sources.title: Geoffrey Chaucer (Q5683), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-02): label 'Geoffrey Chaucer', description '14th century English poet and author (1343-1400)', Korean label 제프리 초서, birth 1343 (year precision) and death 25 October 1400. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Geoffrey Chaucer', opening and early-life sections read (the fetched copy ends mid-article at The Book of the Duchess). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: the outstanding English poet before William Shakespeare, whose masterpiece The Canterbury Tales 'ranks as one of the greatest poetic works in the English language'; he also contributed to the management of public affairs as courtier, diplomat and civil servant under three kings, but it is his avocation, poetry, for which he is remembered; his works are characterised by variety of subject, genre, tone and style; he became competent in French, Latin and Italian and his writings show close familiarity with many important books; The Book of the Duchess (c.1369-70) shows 'originality in combining dream-vision with elegy', tactful use of a first-person narrator who 'both is and is not the poet himself', and skill in presenting natural conversation within Middle English verse. Encyclopedia; admiring, retrospective.

Poetry Foundation, 'Geoffrey Chaucer' biography, read in full: wrote in the English vernacular when Latin and French dominated; his early poems rest on a French base, and trips to Genoa, Florence and Lombardy (1372-73, 1378) developed an interest in Italian that shaped Troilus and Criseyde (from Boccaccio's Il Filostrato); The Parliament of Birds assigns a distinctive voice to each class of bird and 'presages The Canterbury Tales'; the Tales use the frame-tale technique of the Decameron but with tale-tellers from the middle classes who answer ('quite') the previous teller, with tales interrupted or left unfinished; the author notes that he created innocent, bookish self-portraits in the early dream poems unlike 'the canny businessman and social climber he actually was'; the Tales left unfinished, perhaps because the task was too large (about 24 of a planned 120 tales; the Foundation says he was 'not one quarter through his original plan'); the 'Retraction' disclaims his impious works. Poetry organisation biography (literary-critical); its political-career passages are not used.

Academy of American Poets (poets.org), 'About Geoffrey Chaucer', read in full: joined the invasion of France in 1359, was captured and ransomed in 1360; travelled on missions to Italy in 1372 and 1378 where he 'discovered the works of Dante, Giovanni Boccaccio and Petrarch', each of which 'greatly influenced' him; early work shaped by French love poetry, transitional Italian-influenced works include Anelida and Arcite, the Parliament of Fowls and Troilus and Criseyde; the General Prologue of the Canterbury Tales marks his maturity, on which he worked most likely until his death in 1400; 'considered a cultural touchstone' and now the 'Father of English literature'; wrote in the English vernacular while court poetry was written in Anglo-Norman or Latin; the decasyllabic couplet of the Tales later evolved into the heroic couplet and he is credited with pioneering the regular use of iambic pentameter; buried in Westminster Abbey, whose Poets' Corner tradition began with Spenser's burial nearby in 1599. Poetry organisation biography; retrospective praise.

World History Encyclopedia, 'Geoffrey Chaucer' (Joshua J. Mark), read: poet best known for The Canterbury Tales; none of his pieces was published in his lifetime but hand-copied by scribes, and he did not make a living from his writing; he translated the Romance of the Rose (c.1368-72) and Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy (1380s); credited with establishing Middle English as a respectable literary medium and with introducing the rime royal stanza; quoting Larry Benson, 'Chaucer was most prolific as a writer when he was apparently most busy with other affairs'; he completed ten stories of the Legend of Good Women and left it unfinished, and wrote 24 tales of the planned 120; the French poet Eustache Deschamps wrote him a ballad of tribute c.1385; the Canterbury Tales are 'invaluable' as a snapshot of medieval life. Popular reference; some claims (such as the invention of St Valentine's Day) are speculation and are not used.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, eleventh edition (1911), 'Chaucer, Geoffrey', as reproduced on Luminarium (luminarium.org/medlit/chaucerbio.htm), read for the documentary record and reception: household accounts of Elizabeth, countess of Ulster, for 1357 and Edward III's contribution to his ransom in 1360 (documentary entries), his 1386 deposition in the Scrope-Grosvenor case, the royal grants and the 1399 lease at Westminster, burial in Westminster Abbey, the description of the Hoccleve portrait made by his disciple; on reception, that successive copyists reduced his text to a state in which lines could be scanned only by accident, so that 'for fully three centuries his reputation was sustained solely by his narrative power', that over sixty fifteenth-century manuscripts of the Canterbury Tales survive, and that Caxton printed his minor poems and the Canterbury Tales (1478); it also argues his service to the English language is that he proved English 'was sufficient' for poetry, noting Gower had used the best English of his day too. Older scholarly reference reading the archival records; the independent, partly critical voice. Its biographical political details are not used.

Chaucer, 'Chaucers Wordes unto Adam, His Owne Scriveyn' (seven-line poem), Chaucer's Works edited by Walter W. Skeat, Volume I, Wikisource, read: Chaucer rebukes his copyist Adam, saying that if he has to copy Boece or Troilus again he should suffer the scall, that he must 'so ofte a daye' correct and 'rubbe and scrape' the work because of the scribe's 'negligence and rape' (haste), and asks him to 'wryte trewe'. Chaucer's own words, so self-report; used only for what he describes himself doing, never as sole support for a row.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_chaucer_brit, src_chaucer_pf, src_chaucer_poets, src_chaucer_whe, src_chaucer_eb1911 | c.1369-1400 | encyclopedia, poetry organisation, popular reference, older scholarly reference] Britannica credits The Book of the Duchess with 'originality in combining dream-vision with elegy', a tactful narrator who 'both is and is not the poet himself' and natural-sounding conversation in Middle English verse; the Poetry Foundation says the Canterbury Tales adapt the Decameron's frame but fill it with middle-class tellers who answer one another, a new conception of fiction; the Academy of American Poets credits the decasyllabic couplet and regular iambic pentameter, and the World History Encyclopedia the rime royal stanza. Counter-weights: the 1911 Britannica says his French and Italian models supplied his stanza forms and that Gower also used the best English of his day, and the 'first' and 'pioneered' claims are retrospective praise by modern reference works; the sources describe finished works but none documents the process of invention. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.55 to 66 / 0.50 because most support is retrospective canon-building praise and the older scholarly source shows the stanzas and the vernacular choice had French and English precedents.

experimentation.rationale: [src_chaucer_brit, src_chaucer_pf, src_chaucer_poets | c.1370-1400 | encyclopedia, poetry organisation] Britannica notes the variety of his subject matter, genre, tone and style; the Poetry Foundation describes his experiments across dream vision (Book of the Duchess, House of Fame, Parliament of Birds), a seven-line pentameter stanza first used in the Parliament of Birds, the Italian-influenced Troilus and Criseyde, and in the Canterbury Tales different voices for each class of pilgrim, tales that interrupt each other and tales left open, devices it links to questions of closure now central to narratology. It is a documented pattern of trying new forms and registers but the dating of his works is uncertain (the Foundation says so), the sources are interpretive and admiring, and no source records how he tested or discarded alternatives.

curiosity.rationale: [src_chaucer_brit, src_chaucer_poets, src_chaucer_pf, src_chaucer_whe | c.1368-1385 | encyclopedia, poetry organisation, popular reference] Britannica says his writings show close familiarity with many important books and that he became competent in Latin and Italian; the Academy of American Poets says that on trips to Italy in 1372 and 1378 he discovered Dante, Boccaccio and Petrarch and was greatly influenced by them, and the Poetry Foundation traces Troilus and Criseyde to Boccaccio's Il Filostrato; the World History Encyclopedia lists his translations of the Romance of the Rose and of Boethius. The reading and translating are documented through his works, but the interest is inferred from the borrowings and his reasons are not recorded; the trips were official missions, so the contact was not his own initiative, and the row stays low-confidence.

persistence.rationale: [src_chaucer_whe, src_chaucer_pf, src_chaucer_poets | c.1375-1400 | popular reference, poetry organisation] The World History Encyclopedia (quoting the Chaucer scholar Larry Benson) says he was most prolific as a writer when he was busiest with other duties, and the Poetry Foundation and the Academy of American Poets say he worked on the Canterbury Tales over about ten years or more, most likely to his death in 1400, yet wrote only about 24 of a planned 120 tales and left the Legend of Good Women unfinished after ten stories. Sustained work alongside other duties is documented; the unfinished state of the major projects is the cost side (hence dual-edged) and the reasons for stopping are speculation, so confidence is low.

portrait.source: Sixteenth-century portrait of Chaucer by an unknown English artist, folio 1 of the manuscript 'Portrait and Life of Chaucer', British Library, Add. MS 5141 (BL image ID 021444). The British Library's caption names the sitter. It is a later image made about a century and a half after Chaucer died, not a likeness from life. The file is a crop of the folio from head to waist, taken at original resolution from a 1277 x 1994 pixel copy of the library's digital image, with no scaling or upscaling.

PORTRAIT: British Library, 'Portrait and Life of Chaucer', Add. MS 5141, f.1, a sixteenth-century (England) full-length portrait of Chaucer with his arms at top left (BL caption 'Portrait of Chaucer'); the BL's own record text (ID 021444) was read on the live Flickr page https://www.flickr.com/photos/britishlibrary/12458941013/ (uploaded 11 Feb 2014 by the British Library; licence field 'No known copyright restrictions'; the BL names the sitter in its caption and offers paid high-quality copies through Images Online, which is a service, not a licence on the content). The BL's own website pages were unavailable (a cyber-attack notice replaces the content), so I could not read a BL web page for the manuscript; Commons File:Portrait of Chaucer - Portrait and Life of Chaucer (16th C), f.1 - BL Add MS 5141.jpg (1277 x 1994 px, Cc-zero tag, uploaded by GWToolset from the same BL Flickr photo) was read as a cross-check only. RIGHTS BASIS: a sixteenth-century miniature by an unknown English artist, public domain by age everywhere; the digital reproduction is a faithful photograph of a two-dimensional work, which adds no new copyright in the US; the BL's Flickr release carries no restriction and the Commons CC0 tag agrees with the Flickr page, so there is no licence conflict. I did NOT rely on the Commons tag or on 'no known restrictions' alone. The image was downloaded with curl from Commons (1277 x 1994 original) and CROPPED (not scaled) to the figure from head to waist, 800 x 1000 px, so the face is visible; the BL museum stamp and the folio frame are cropped away; no upscaling. kind historical_depiction: a posthumous sixteenth-century image of a sitter who died in 1400, not a likeness taken from life (the Hoccleve portrait of c.1412 in Harley 4866, f.88, is an earlier alternative whose only copy I found was a Commons upload of a Harvard web page, so it was not used).
